published_title: THE BRIDGE THAT MISSED BY NINE METRES

story.title: THE BRIDGE THAT MISSED BY NINE METRES
story.deck: Two villages built a bridge from opposite banks and met nine metres apart. Each swears the other sighted wrong, and Illuminara has ten days to find out what both of them measured.
story.shape: Six scenes across ten days and one frosty morning: a builder's accusation at the north tip, a ferry crossing and two survey books that agree with themselves, the numbers that add up to nine, a table where three designs are refused, a lowering against a rising river, and a joint that is read aloud every winter.

scenes.title: Nine Metres
paragraphs: *Upper Wend, the north tip of the bridge · dawn, ten days before the flood*

Two half-bridges stood out over the river like the hands of people who had agreed to shake and then thought better of it. Between the tips lay nine metres of brown water. A string stretched from rail to rail would also have shown the north span pointing nine centimetres left of the south, and that was the part that made the villages shout.

Illuminara walked out along Odo's side over decking so new it still smelled of larch. Odo of Upper Wend followed with a notebook held against his chest, the way a man holds a shield he expects to be asked to put down.

**Odo**  
I set my line from the Tithe Stone. The same stone Hanne Sull used. I closed it to a centimetre, twice. You are going to tell me she sighted wrong. I will carry you over the river on my back if you can show it.

**Illuminara**  
I am not going to tell you that yet. I want to know what each of you would have to be wrong about, and I want to see it myself. Ten days to the flood. After it the ferry will not run until April. Upper Wend has eleven women due before then, and one midwife, who lives on the other bank.

**Odo**  
Seren Ashby. I have known Seren since she was nine. Do you think I need reminding?

**Illuminara**  
No. I think you needed someone to say it, so you would not have to say it first.
He looked at her, then at the water, the way you look at a debt.

**Odo**  
If you say we were both right, you are saying the river lied. Rivers do not lie. Somebody sighted wrong, and it was not us.

She did not argue. Behind the anger stood a man who had spent two summers lifting beams to a line he trusted with his name, and she would not take it from him before there was something to put in its place.

**Illuminara**  
Then show me how you sighted. Slowly, as though I were new. I will do exactly what you say.
Nobody had asked Odo to teach anything since the closing day. He set down the notebook, took the sighting vane out of his coat, and began.

scenes.title: Two True Lines
paragraphs: *Lower Wend, the south landing and the survey shed · midday*

The ferry was a flat raft on a rope, poled by its keeper, Pell Garrow, with the patience of a man paid by the crossing. Halfway over, the rope stopped taking the weight and a length of old anchor chain took over, rattling through the sheave. Illuminara watched it pass through the block and noticed that she had noticed.
Seren Ashby was waiting on the landing with a leather bag at her feet, sixty years old and solid as a gatepost.

**Seren**  
Eleven in Upper Wend before March, and I have caught nine of the last ten. If you are here to be moved by my courage, save yourself the trouble. I would rather walk.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will try to get you something to walk on.

Hanne Sull ran her survey the way she ran her tea, strong and measured to the gram. Each page of her survey book began with the weather drawn small in ink: a sun, a cloud, one grim little rain. She taught Illuminara the chain, the plumb, the vane and the arithmetic of closing a line, and watched with folded arms while the visitor did everything wrong and then right.

By evening Illuminara had re-run both crews' work with the crews' own hands. The north line closed to eight millimetres, the south to six. She laid the two books side by side on the shed table and could find no error in either larger than a thumbnail.

**Hanne**  
I told Odo that in July. He said it was impossible, which is what people say when it is not impossible.

**Illuminara**  
It is not. Both lines are good, so the lines are not what moved. You each began from one place. What was it?

**Hanne**  
The Tithe Stone, on the north terrace. On rock. It cannot have moved.
She stopped, pen lifted.

**Hanne**  
Last April it came out nine centimetres off my line. I wrote it down as chain stretch. Chains stretch.

Alone in the dusk, Illuminara laid her palm on the south footing and then, crossing, on the north. Both gave the same message, the way a rope tells you someone is pulling the other end: two great blocks either side of nothing, each drawn gently away from the other. A feeling was a hypothesis, and nobody was going to hang a bridge from her palm.

scenes.title: The Sum
paragraphs: *The ferry landing, Lower Wend · evening, the fourth day*

The test was cheap and could embarrass her. If the valley had opened, it would have left marks: cracks in orchard walls, steps in lanes, doors that stuck last winter and were blamed on frost. She had asked each builder to measure the other's bank, every crack and every step, and bring back one number.

Odo had gone south at dawn and been escorted through Lower Wend by a dog. Hanne had gone north at noon, set foot in Upper Wend for the first time since the closing day, and asked a child to show her the lane. Now they stood at opposite ends of Pell's raft, the only neutral ground in the valley.

**Odo**  
Three point six. Her orchard wall, the lane by the well, the churchyard step. Eleven cracks.

**Hanne**  
Five point four, in nine. A door in your village sticks so badly the baker climbs through the window.

**Odo**  
He enjoys it.
Nobody said the sum. It lay on the planks between them like a fish.

**Pell**  
Nine.
He had been leaning on the pole with the face of a man deciding whether to confess to a small crime.

**Pell**  
I have pulled this raft on a hundred and eighteen metres of cable for nineteen years. At harvest it parted at the south ring. I spliced it, and the ends would not meet, so I shackled on nine metres of my father's anchor chain and told myself I had measured wrong. A ferryman who miscounts does not advertise it.

Illuminara waited. Two measurements, made by people who disliked one another with no tape in common, had landed on one number. Had she been wrong, the cracks would have summed to nothing and the cable would have fitted.

**Odo**  
So the river did not lie.

**Hanne**  
The valley. It opened at the harvest, while we were stacking sheaves. Each of us built to a true line, and the ground walked off from under it.

**Odo**  
I called you a liar in front of both villages.

**Hanne**  
I called you a worse word. I will think about taking yours back after the bridge stands.
It was not forgiveness and Illuminara did not reach for it. It was the first sentence either of them had said to the other that included the word *after*.

scenes.title: Three Designs, Refused
paragraphs: *The north abutment shed · evening, day six, rain on the tarpaulin*

They sat at one table, which had taken six days and a great deal of tea. Odo drew on the back of a seed catalogue, Hanne in the margin of her survey book, and Pell held the lamp and a mug of something he called medicinal.

**Odo**  
We lengthen my span by nine metres. A new pier, a new beam. Twelve weeks.

**Hanne**  
The flood is in four days. Mine is the barges: moor the Marl and the Teasel nose to tail across the gap and call it a pontoon.

**Odo**  
The first crest takes it. And the ice takes what the crest leaves.

**Hanne**  
And twelve weeks takes Seren's winter, Odo.
They both turned, with something like relief, to the visitor who could have ended the argument in an afternoon.

**Illuminara**  
I can swing a twelve-metre beam across the gap, set it on both tips and be gone by dinner. I am saying it aloud so that you can say no.

**Hanne**  
No.

**Odo**  
No. Then it is yours, and when it cracks in March you will be somewhere three skies away, and who do we shout at?

**Hanne**  
A bridge that nobody here built is a bridge nobody here can mend.
Illuminara wrote *not mine* on the catalogue and underlined it. She felt, absurdly, as if she had been given something.

**Illuminara**  
You are both designing for the valley you surveyed. Design for the one that exists. A bridge that expects to be pulled, and is not frightened when it is.

**Pell**  
Then a floated span? You bring the beam in on the barges at a rising river, and you do not lift it. You settle it.

It took the evening to turn a ferryman's guess into a design. Hanne knew barges and mill sluices, where a timber rides in a slot so a frame can move without cracking. Odo knew what a bearing could stand. Hanne drew the slot; Odo made it forty centimetres at each end, because the valley had opened nine metres in a night and nine centimetres since April, and he would not be the man who built a bridge that assumed it had stopped.

**Hanne**  
The slot closes by a hand's width, we meet. Both crews. Nobody waits for the village council.

**Odo**  
And the stop. If the staff on Pell's landing reads one point nine, the span does not go. Either of us rings the bell twice, and the barges are cut loose.

**Illuminara**  
Then that bell is yours, not mine. If it rings twice I go home. And this is all I can do, so plan around it: I can hold the two barges against the current for forty minutes. Not the beam. The lines carry the beam. I take the shocks. After that I am no more use than a sack of grain.

**Hanne**  
Forty minutes is enough if we do not argue.

**Odo**  
We will not argue.
Pell, who had known them both for nineteen years, raised his medicinal mug and said nothing at all.

scenes.title: The Lowering
paragraphs: *The gap, midstream · afternoon, day nine*

The river was rising at six centimetres an hour and the staff on the landing read one point six two. Sixteen people on each bank held the lines. The Marl and the Teasel lay lashed side by side with the box beam riding between them, twelve metres of larch and iron that two villages had built in three days, nose upstream and trembling in the current like a horse that has seen a ghost.

Illuminara went into the water at the bows. It was colder than she had decided to expect. She laid a palm on each barge and felt the river lean on them, a crowd with a single bad idea, and she leaned back.

**Hanne**  
Scuppers on my word. Odo, the pins.

**Odo**  
Pins ready.
At one point seven four an alder came down the middle of the river with its root-plate up, turning slowly, and every head on both banks turned with it.

**Odo**  
One bell.
He rang it once. Everyone froze. On the south bank Hanne's crew swung out a boom pole and walked the trunk off the Teasel's quarter with a long, rude, patient shove, and the bell was silent.

**Hanne**  
Clear.

Illuminara counted minutes in the weight on her hands. Eleven. Fourteen. At twenty, the river tried something different, a sidelong shove from the south, and she took it in the arms and the spine and gave nothing back.

**Pell**  
One point seven eight.

**Hanne**  
Scuppers. Open.

**Odo**  
Settle.

The barges sank, very slowly, under the weight of the water they had been told to take, and the beam went down with them with a sound like a very large animal breathing out. The north bearing met the north tip. The south bearing met the south. The slot took the first of its forty centimetres of travel with a small, clean tick.

**Odo**  
Pin.

**Hanne**  
Pinned.
At thirty-seven minutes the lines came off. The Teasel, released, slewed, found the current and went away downriver, riding high and empty, and Hanne watched her go and said nothing for a long time.

**Odo**  
I will build you another.

**Hanne**  
You will build me a better one. Come to my yard on Thursday.

Illuminara climbed the bank on shaking legs and sat in the mud. At dusk Seren Ashby came to the north tip with her leather bag. She waited until Odo and Hanne had walked it twice, then went out onto the span, stopped where the beam met the tip, and set one boot across the dark seam. The plank moved a hair under her. She nodded to it as one might to a horse. Then she walked into Upper Wend, and no one said anything, because nothing larger could be said.

scenes.title: The Slot
paragraphs: *The bridge, midspan · five weeks later, hard frost*

The crest had come at two point six on the staff and gone, and the bridge had stood it with water slapping the soffit and every pin in its place. Seren had crossed six times since. The Wend ferry, retired to the bank, had a small boy asleep in it.

A week ago a tremor, smaller than the one at harvest, had walked through the valley. Pell had come out on the bridge with a bucket of hot water for his hands and a tape and found the slot a little narrower. Now, on the first morning with ice on the rails, the two crews stood at midspan with their hands in their sleeves, and Illuminara stood slightly to one side, having been asked to come and not asked to do anything.

**Odo**  
Thirty-seven.

**Hanne**  
Thirty-seven. It started at forty. Three centimetres, in a week.

**Odo**  
Then the valley is not done.

**Hanne**  
No. And the bridge is not, either. When it reads ten, we come.
Illuminara laid her palm on the beam, out of habit. Hanne watched her do it.

**Hanne**  
We have a tape.

**Illuminara**  
I know. I wanted to feel it.

**Hanne**  
Feel it afterwards.

The book on the rail was the bridge-warden's book, which had two hands in it already, Odo's square and Hanne's flat, and a third in the margin, Pell's, who had been named warden by both villages and been paid by both, to his visible alarm. Odo read the figure aloud, Hanne wrote it, and each of them signed beneath it, once.

**Seren**  
Marta's boy came on Tuesday. I walked.

She went by them with her bag, with the plank ringing very faintly under her step. They were not friends. They were two people who had agreed to read the same tape, and over a gap that had once been nine metres, that was enough to walk on.

scenes.title: The Slot
paragraphs: *The bridge, midspan · five weeks later, hard frost*

The crest had come at two point six on the staff and gone, and the bridge had stood it with water slapping the soffit and every pin in its place. Seren had crossed six times since. The Wend ferry, retired to the bank, had a small boy asleep in it.

A week ago a tremor, smaller than the one at harvest, had walked through the valley. Pell had come out on the bridge with a bucket of hot water for his hands and a tape and found the slot a little narrower. Now, on the first morning with ice on the rails, the two crews stood at midspan with their hands in their sleeves, and Illuminara stood slightly to one side, having been asked to come and not asked to do anything.

**Odo**  
Thirty-seven.

**Hanne**  
Thirty-seven. It started at forty. Three centimetres, in a week.

**Odo**  
Then the valley is not done.

**Hanne**  
No. And the bridge is not, either. When it reads ten, we come.
Illuminara laid her palm on the beam, out of habit. Hanne watched her do it.

**Hanne**  
We have a tape.

**Illuminara**  
I know. I wanted to feel it.

**Hanne**  
Feel it afterwards.

The book on the rail was the bridge-warden's book, which had two hands in it already, Odo's square and Hanne's flat, and a third in the margin, Pell's, who had been named warden by both villages and been paid by both, to his visible alarm. Odo read the figure aloud, Hanne wrote it, and each of them signed beneath it, once.

**Seren**  
Marta's boy came on Tuesday. I walked.

She went by them with her bag, with the plank ringing very faintly under her step. They were not friends. They were two people who had agreed to read the same tape, and over a gap that had once been nine metres, that was enough to walk on.

story.title: THE BRIDGE THAT MISSED BY NINE METRES
story.deck: Two villages built a bridge from opposite banks and met nine metres apart. Each swears the other sighted wrong, and Illuminara has ten days to find out what both of them measured.
story.shape: Six scenes across ten days and one frosty morning: a builder's accusation at the north tip, a ferry crossing and two survey books that agree with themselves, the old stones and the cable that add up to nine, a table where three designs are refused, a lowering against a river that rises faster than forecast, and a joint that is read aloud every winter.

scenes.title: Nine Metres
paragraphs: *Upper Wend, the north tip of the bridge · dawn, ten days before the flood*

Two half-bridges stood out over the river like the hands of people who had agreed to shake and then thought better of it. Between the tips lay nine metres of brown water. A string stretched from rail to rail would also have shown the north span pointing nine centimetres left of the south, and that was the part that made the villages shout.

Illuminara walked out along Odo's side over decking so new it still smelled of larch. Odo of Upper Wend followed with a notebook held against his chest, the way a man holds a shield he expects to be asked to put down.

**Odo**  
I set my line from the Tithe Stone. The same stone Hanne Sull used. I closed it to a centimetre, twice. You are going to tell me she sighted wrong. I will carry you over the river on my back if you can show it.

**Illuminara**  
I am not going to tell you that yet. I want to know what each of you would have to be wrong about, and I want to see it myself. Ten days to the flood. After it the ferry will not run until April. Upper Wend has eleven women due before then, and one midwife, who lives on the other bank.

**Odo**  
Seren Ashby. I have known Seren since she was nine. Do you think I need reminding?

**Illuminara**  
No. I think you needed someone to say it, so you would not have to say it first.
He looked at her, then at the water, the way you look at a debt.

**Odo**  
If you say we were both right, you are saying the river lied. Rivers do not lie. Somebody sighted wrong, and it was not us.

She did not argue. Behind the anger stood a man who had spent two summers lifting beams to a line he trusted with his name, and she would not take it from him before there was something to put in its place.

**Illuminara**  
Then show me how you sighted. Slowly, as though I were new. I will do exactly what you say.
Nobody had asked Odo to teach anything since the closing day. He set down the notebook, took the sighting vane out of his coat, and began.

scenes.title: Two True Lines
paragraphs: *Lower Wend, the south landing and the survey shed · midday*

The ferry was a flat raft on a rope, poled by its keeper, Pell Garrow, with the patience of a man paid by the crossing. Halfway over, the rope stopped taking the weight and a length of old anchor chain took over, rattling through the sheave. Illuminara watched it pass through the block and noticed that she had noticed.
Seren Ashby was waiting on the landing with a leather bag at her feet, sixty years old and solid as a gatepost.

**Seren**  
Eleven in Upper Wend before March, and I have caught nine of the last ten. If you are here to be moved by my courage, save yourself the trouble. I would rather walk.

**Illuminara**  
Then I will try to get you something to walk on.

Hanne Sull ran her survey the way she ran her tea, strong and measured to the gram. Each page of her survey book began with the weather drawn small in ink: a sun, a cloud, one grim little rain. She taught Illuminara the chain, the plumb, the vane and the arithmetic of closing a line, and watched with folded arms while the visitor did everything wrong and then right.

By evening Illuminara had re-run both crews' work with the crews' own hands. The north line closed to eight millimetres, the south to six. She laid the two books side by side on the shed table and could find no error in either larger than a thumbnail.

**Hanne**  
I told Odo that in July. He said it was impossible, which is what people say when it is not impossible.

**Illuminara**  
It is not. Both lines are good, so the lines are not what moved. You each began from one place. What was it?

**Hanne**  
The Tithe Stone, on the north terrace. On rock. It cannot have moved.
She stopped, pen lifted.

**Hanne**  
Last April my foresight to the south pier came out nine centimetres off the stone's line. I wrote it down as chain stretch. Chains stretch.

**Illuminara**  
The stone is on rock, so it did not walk. What stands on something that can?

**Hanne**  
The meadows. The flats between the terrace and the water. Nobody lives on them. We only cross them.

**Illuminara**  
Is there anything down there that belongs to neither of you?

**Hanne**  
The tithe-stones. One every hundred paces down each lane to the ford, set before either village kept a warden, and written in the parish book. The bridge is laid on the ford's line.

**Illuminara**  
Then the stones are a tape nobody here owns.

Alone in the dusk, Illuminara laid her palm on the south footing and then, crossing, on the north. Both gave the same message, the way a rope tells you someone is pulling the other end: two great blocks either side of nothing, each drawn gently away from the other. A feeling was a hypothesis, and nobody was going to hang a bridge from her palm.

scenes.title: The Sum
paragraphs: *The ferry landing, Lower Wend · evening, the fourth day*

The test was cheap and could embarrass her. If the ground between the rock and the river had stretched, the old stones would say so. They stood a hundred paces apart down each lane, they were written in the parish book, and they belonged to neither crew. She had asked each builder to re-chain the other's bank stone by stone, set the length against the book, and bring back one number.

Odo had gone south at dawn and been escorted through Lower Wend by a dog. Hanne had gone north at noon, set foot in Upper Wend for the first time since the closing day, and asked a child to show her the lane. Now they stood at opposite ends of Pell's raft, the only neutral ground in the valley.

**Odo**  
Three point six. From the south terrace to the water, her lane is longer than the book says by that much. Eleven cracks and steps hold some of it: the orchard wall, the lane by the well, the churchyard step. The rest is in the clay.

**Hanne**  
Five point four, in yours, the same way. A door in your low lane sticks so badly the baker climbs through the window.

**Odo**  
He enjoys it.
Nobody said the sum. It lay on the planks between them like a fish.

**Pell**  
Nine.
He had been leaning on the pole with the face of a man deciding whether to confess to a small crime.

**Pell**  
I have pulled this raft on a hundred and eighteen metres of cable for nineteen years. At harvest it parted at the south ring. I spliced it, and the ends would not meet, so I shackled on nine metres of my father's anchor chain and told myself I had measured wrong. A ferryman who miscounts does not advertise it.

**Illuminara**  
Taut or slack, when you measured? Spliced, or sagged?

**Pell**  
Taut as a harp. Three times, mostly hoping to prove myself wrong.

Illuminara waited. Two measurements, made by people who disliked one another, against stones neither of them owned, had landed on one number, and a third, made by a man who had hoped to be wrong, had landed on it too. Had she been mistaken, the stones would have agreed with the book and the cable would have fitted.

**Odo**  
So the river did not lie.

**Hanne**  
The valley. It opened at the harvest, while we were stacking sheaves. Each of us built to a true line, and the ground walked off from under it.

**Illuminara**  
Through the meadows, not through the villages.

**Hanne**  
The houses stand on rock. Nobody noticed, because nobody lives in a meadow. The bridge was the only thing we had built on one.

**Odo**  
I called you a liar in front of both villages.

**Hanne**  
I called you a worse word. I will think about taking yours back after the bridge stands.
It was not forgiveness and Illuminara did not reach for it. It was the first sentence either of them had said to the other that included the word *after*.

scenes.title: Three Designs, Refused
paragraphs: *The north abutment shed · evening, day six, rain on the tarpaulin*

They sat at one table, which had taken six days and a great deal of tea. Odo drew on the back of a seed catalogue, Hanne in the margin of her survey book, and Pell held the lamp and a mug of something he called medicinal.

**Odo**  
We lengthen my span by nine metres. A new pier, a new beam. Twelve weeks.

**Hanne**  
The flood is in four days. Mine is the barges: moor the Marl and the Teasel nose to tail across the gap and call it a pontoon.

**Odo**  
The first crest takes it. And the ice takes what the crest leaves.

**Hanne**  
And twelve weeks takes Seren's winter, Odo.
They both turned, with something like relief, to the visitor who could have ended the argument in an afternoon.

**Illuminara**  
I can swing a twelve-metre beam across the gap, set it on both tips and be gone by dinner. I am saying it aloud so that you can say no.

**Hanne**  
No.

**Odo**  
No. Then it is yours, and when it cracks in March you will be somewhere three skies away, and who do we shout at?

**Hanne**  
A bridge that nobody here built is a bridge nobody here can mend.
Illuminara wrote *not mine* on the catalogue and underlined it. She felt, absurdly, as if she had been given something.

**Illuminara**  
You are both designing for the valley you surveyed. Design for the one that exists. A bridge that expects to be pulled, and is not frightened when it is.

**Pell**  
Then a floated span? You bring the beam in on the barges at a rising river, and you do not lift it. You settle it.

It took the evening to turn a ferryman's guess into a design. Hanne knew barges and mill sluices, where a timber rides in a slot so a frame can move without cracking. Odo knew what a bearing could stand. Hanne drew the slot; Odo made it forty centimetres at each end, because the valley had opened nine metres in a night and nine centimetres since April, and he would not be the man who built a bridge that assumed it had stopped.

**Hanne**  
The slot closes by a hand's width, we meet. Both crews. Nobody waits for the village council.

**Odo**  
And the stop. If the staff on Pell's landing reads one point nine, the span does not go. Either of us rings the bell twice, and the barges are cut loose.

**Illuminara**  
Then that bell is yours, not mine. If it rings twice I go home. And this is all I can do, so plan around it: I can hold the two barges against the current for forty minutes. Not the beam. The lines carry the beam. I take the shocks. After that I am no more use than a sack of grain.

**Hanne**  
Forty minutes is enough if we do not argue.

**Odo**  
We will not argue.
Pell, who had known them both for nineteen years, raised his medicinal mug and said nothing at all.

scenes.title: The Lowering
paragraphs: *The gap, midstream · afternoon, day nine*

The river was rising at six centimetres an hour and the staff on the landing read one point six two. Sixteen people on each bank held the lines, two sets of them crossed, bow to opposite stern, so that neither barge could walk ahead of the other. The Marl and the Teasel lay side by side in the gap, nose upstream, with a hand's breadth of brown water between them, and the box beam rode across both on its cradles: twelve metres of larch and iron that two villages had built in three days, a metre and a half of it over each tip, trembling in the current like a horse that has seen a ghost.

Illuminara went into the water at the bows. It was colder than she had decided to expect. She laid a palm on each barge and felt the river lean on them, a crowd with a single bad idea, and she leaned back.

**Hanne**  
Valves shut, tanks dry. Freeboard?

**Odo**  
Forty centimetres on the Marl, with the beam aboard.

**Hanne**  
Forty on the Teasel. That floats the beam twice over, so one sticking valve will not sink us. Level to the hand.

**Odo**  
Cross-lines taut. Pins ready.

**Pell**  
One point six three.
It was what six an hour promised. At the tenth minute an alder came down the middle of the river with its root-plate up, turning slowly, and every head on both banks turned with it.

**Odo**  
One bell.
He rang it once. Everyone froze. On the south bank Hanne's crew swung out a boom pole and walked the trunk off the Teasel's quarter with a long, rude, patient shove, and the bell was silent.

**Hanne**  
Clear.

**Pell**  
One point six six.
He said it twice, because the first time nobody wanted it.

**Pell**  
Three centimetres since the tree, and four minutes of them. That is not six an hour. That is forty-five. The water is brown with rain I cannot see.
Hanne did the sum aloud, because someone had to, and Odo did it after her to see that it matched.

**Hanne**  
Valves at twenty-four minutes, beam seated by thirty-three, pins by thirty-five, lines off at thirty-seven. The staff will read one point eight three.

**Odo**  
Seven under the line. Nine minutes of river we do not own.

**Hanne**  
Then nobody opens a valve late.

**Illuminara**  
I have forty minutes. You are asking me for thirty-seven.

**Hanne**  
I am asking you for thirty-seven.

Nobody rang. Illuminara counted minutes in the weight on her hands. Sixteen. Eighteen. At twenty, the river tried something different, a sidelong shove from the south, and she took it in the arms and the spine and gave nothing back.

**Pell**  
One point seven four.

**Hanne**  
Valves. Open, together, on my count. Three. Two. One.

The barges sank, very slowly, under the weight of the water they had been told to take, and the cross-lines creaked and held, and the beam went down with them with a sound like a very large animal breathing out. It took nine minutes, and nobody afterwards called them short. The north bearing met the north tip. The south bearing met the south. The slot took the first of its forty centimetres of travel with a small, clean tick.

**Odo**  
North home. I have a hand under the shoe: seated.

**Hanne**  
South home. Daylight under both cradles.

**Odo**  
Pin.

**Hanne**  
Pinned.

**Pell**  
One point eight two.

**Hanne**  
Cross-lines off. Marl first, then the Teasel. Slack, not pull. There is nothing holding that beam up now but the stone.

At thirty-seven minutes the lines came off. The Marl came out clean from under the span, stern first, hauled by the north crew. The Teasel, pumped light as she cleared, slewed, found the current and went away downriver, riding high and empty, and Hanne watched her go and said nothing for a long time.

**Odo**  
I will build you another.

**Hanne**  
You will build me a better one. Come to my yard on Thursday.

Illuminara climbed the bank on shaking legs and sat in the mud. At dusk Seren Ashby came to the north tip with her leather bag. She waited until Odo and Hanne had walked it twice, then went out onto the span, stopped where the beam met the tip, and set one boot across the dark seam. The plank moved a hair under her. She nodded to it as one might to a horse. Then she walked into Upper Wend, and no one said anything, because nothing larger could be said.
